event_overview.title: About Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.subject: Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.summary: This event concerns an effort in the U.S. House of Representatives to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth through articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie. Impeachment is a constitutional process in which the House may formally charge federal civil officers, while the Senate alone conducts any subsequent trial; it is separate from criminal prosecution.

facts.label: Constitutional authority
facts.value: The U.S. Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments.

facts.label: Who may be impeached
facts.value: The Constitution makes the President, Vice President, and other civil officers of the United States subject to impeachment for treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors; a Cabinet secretary is a federal civil officer.

facts.label: House and Senate thresholds
facts.value: The House approves articles of impeachment by a simple majority. If articles are transmitted, the Senate considers the case, and conviction requires the concurrence of two-thirds of senators present.

facts.label: Possible consequences
facts.value: A Senate conviction can remove an official from office and may include disqualification from future federal office; it does not bar separate criminal indictment, trial, or punishment.

facts.label: Current House effort
facts.value: On November 9, 2026, Massie presented an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. Reporting described the measure as raising allegations concerning war-powers and other conduct; those allegations are the basis of the proposed articles, not findings of guilt.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the November 9-10, 2026 developments surrounding the proposed House action and Hegseth's response, not a complete account of the underlying allegations, House deliberations, or any possible Senate trial.

explore_lenses.title: The resolution reaches beyond the Iran war
explore_lenses.summary: Massie’s 34-page resolution centers on alleged violations of Congress’s war-powers authority in Iran, but it also raises civilian-harm, maritime-strike, Venezuela, Yemen and speech-related accusations. These are allegations in an impeachment resolution, not findings by a court or congressional trial.

claims.text: The first three articles allege that Hegseth initiated or continued hostilities against Iran without congressional authorization, including after Congress acted to direct the removal of U.S. forces and after the War Powers Resolution time limits cited by Massie.

Other articles accuse Hegseth of weakening Pentagon civilian-casualty safeguards, conducting unlawful killings in maritime counter-drug operations, suppressing a senator’s speech, and involvement in actions concerning Yemen and Venezuela.

Hegseth rejects the charges as policy disputes rather than impeachable offenses, arguing that the operations were lawful and that the effort harms U.S. forces; Speaker Mike Johnson called it a political gambit and predicted it would fail.

explore_lenses.title: A clash over authorization and war-powers deadlines
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate dispute is whether the administration could continue Iran operations without a specific congressional authorization. Massie says it could not; the administration has maintained that hostilities had ended or were covered by a ceasefire, making the statutory timing argument inapplicable.

claims.text: Massie’s resolution says U.S. forces entered hostilities with Iran on February 28, 2026 without a declaration of war, a specific authorization for use of force, or an Iranian attack creating the emergency described in the War Powers Resolution.

Massie’s counterargument is that the Iran conflict continued despite Congress’s June measure directing forces to leave hostilities and despite the resolution’s 60-day limit, with a possible 30-day withdrawal period.

Hegseth called the effort a “farce” and “sabotage,” saying it reflects policy disputes rather than impeachable conduct. The immediate congressional consequence was scheduled consideration on Nov. 10 of a Republican procedural motion to refer Massie’s resolution, not confirmation of a final impeachment vote.

sections.body: The first three articles allege that Hegseth initiated or continued hostilities against Iran without congressional authorization, including after Congress acted to direct U.S. forces out of hostilities and beyond War Powers Resolution deadlines cited by Massie. The resolution says U.S. forces entered hostilities on Feb. 28, 2026, without a declaration of war, a specific authorization or an Iranian attack creating the emergency described in the statute. Other articles allege weakened civilian-casualty protections, unlawful maritime counter-drug killings, suppression of a senator’s speech, and actions concerning Yemen and Venezuela.

sections.heading: War Powers Arguments Remain Contested
sections.body: Reporting on the resolution says the administration told Congress on May 1 that hostilities had ended, while Hegseth told senators that a ceasefire paused or stopped the 60-day clock. Massie argues that the conflict continued despite Congress’s June measure and the statutory limit, which may allow a further 30-day withdrawal period. Hegseth rejects the accusations as policy disagreements, says the operations were lawful and argues that the impeachment push harms U.S. forces; Speaker Mike Johnson called the effort a political gambit and predicted it would fail.

sections.heading: House Procedure Limits Immediate Consequences
sections.body: The House Republican Cloakroom’s schedule listed a procedural motion related to Massie’s resolution, and its vote sheet described the item as a Republican motion to refer it. Even if the House were to approve impeachment, Hegseth would remain in office unless the Senate held a trial and convicted him by a two-thirds vote. AP reported that the timing and subsequent path in the House were uncertain, while Johnson forecast defeat in the Republican-led chamber.

explore_lenses.label: Why does the U.S. absence matter?
explore_lenses.title: A universal review loses the country’s direct response
explore_lenses.summary: The Universal Periodic Review (UPR) is designed to subject every UN member state to peer scrutiny, using government, UN, and civil-society material. The U.S. absence does not erase the evidence submitted about its record, but it prevents U.S. officials from answering questions and responding to recommendations in the normal forum.

claims.text: The UPR reviews each UN member state’s human-rights record roughly every 4.5 years; the process draws on a national report, an OHCHR compilation of UN information, and an OHCHR summary of credible stakeholder submissions.

The U.S. had completed three prior UPR reviews, including its third review in 2020; the State Department previously described the process as distinct from membership in the 47-state Human Rights Council because non-members also participate in reviews.

Human Rights Watch argues that a second U.S. failure to appear is unprecedented in the UPR’s nearly 20-year history and says the Council should not allow the U.S. to be exempted from a process intended to apply to all UN members.

event_overview.title: About Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.subject: Impeachment Proceedings
event_overview.summary: This event concerns an effort in the U.S. House of Representatives to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth through articles introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie. Impeachment is a constitutional process in which the House may formally charge federal civil officers, while the Senate alone conducts any subsequent trial; it is separate from criminal prosecution.

facts.label: Constitutional authority
facts.value: The U.S. Constitution gives the House the sole power to impeach and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments.

facts.label: Who may be impeached
facts.value: The Constitution makes the President, Vice President, and other civil officers of the United States subject to impeachment for treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors; a Cabinet secretary is a federal civil officer.

facts.label: House and Senate thresholds
facts.value: The House approves articles of impeachment by a simple majority. If articles are transmitted, the Senate considers the case, and conviction requires the concurrence of two-thirds of senators present.

facts.label: Possible consequences
facts.value: A Senate conviction can remove an official from office and may include disqualification from future federal office; it does not bar separate criminal indictment, trial, or punishment.

facts.label: Current House effort
facts.value: On November 9, 2026, Massie presented an impeachment resolution against Hegseth. Reporting described the measure as raising allegations concerning war-powers and other conduct; those allegations are the basis of the proposed articles, not findings of guilt.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the November 9-10, 2026 developments surrounding the proposed House action and Hegseth's response, not a complete account of the underlying allegations, House deliberations, or any possible Senate trial.

explore_lenses.label: What does Massie’s resolution actually allege?
explore_lenses.title: Eight articles reach beyond the Iran war
explore_lenses.summary: The proposal is not limited to one allegation about Iran. The text published by Rep. Thomas Massie sets out eight impeachment articles that accuse Hegseth of unlawful uses of force and other alleged abuses of office.

claims.text: The resolution states that it impeaches Defense Secretary Peter Brian Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors” and presents eight articles to the Senate if adopted by the House.
The first articles allege violations of the War Powers Resolution tied to Iran, including that hostilities lacked congressional authorization and continued beyond the statute’s asserted time limits.
Other articles in the published resolution concern alleged actions involving Venezuela and Yemen, so a vote on the measure would concern a broader set of accusations than the Iran operation alone.

explore_lenses.label: What do Massie and Hegseth argue?
explore_lenses.title: They dispute both legality and consequences
explore_lenses.summary: Massie frames the conduct as unlawful war-making without the required congressional role. Hegseth says the operations were lawful, Congress was notified, and impeachment would harm U.S. military missions.

claims.text: Massie’s resolution argues that the Constitution and the War Powers Resolution limit introducing U.S. forces into hostilities without a declaration of war, statutory authorization, or an attack-created national emergency.

The War Powers Resolution provides for termination within 60 days after a qualifying report is submitted or required, absent a declaration of war, specific authorization, a statutory extension, or Congress being unable to meet; it permits up to 30 additional days for certified military necessity during withdrawal.

Hegseth said the Iran, Venezuela, cartel, and Yemen operations were lawful orders of the commander in chief, were communicated to Congress, and were executed by U.S. forces; he characterized the impeachment push as a political spectacle rather than oversight.
President Trump publicly backed Hegseth, while House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said he supported the resolution and accused Hegseth of abusing his position and helping engineer the Iran war.

event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers here to the 2026 armed conflict between the United States and Iran, including U.S. military operations in and against Iran and maritime-security operations around the Strait of Hormuz. The conflict has combined direct military action, disputes over commercial navigation through the strait, and U.S. congressional debate over the President’s authority to continue hostilities.

facts.label: Start of U.S. operation
facts.value: U.S. Central Command says it began Operation Epic Fury against Iran on February 28, 2026, at the President’s direction.

facts.label: Geographic focus
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf of Oman and the Persian Gulf, has been a central operational area; CENTCOM described it as an international sea passage and a key trade corridor while conducting mine-clearance and shipping-security operations.

facts.label: Stated U.S. military objectives
facts.value: The White House said the February 28 operation was directed at Iran’s ballistic-missile and drone capabilities, navy, and defense-industrial base; these are stated U.S. objectives, not an independent assessment of the conflict’s effects.

facts.label: Maritime escalation
facts.value: CENTCOM said U.S. strikes beginning July 7 followed attacks on neutral-flagged commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on July 6–7, with targets including missile sites, air defenses, maritime assets, support infrastructure, and command-and-control capabilities.

facts.label: U.S. war-powers framework
facts.value: Under the War Powers Resolution, the President generally must terminate a reported use of U.S. armed forces within 60 days unless Congress declares war, specifically authorizes the use, extends the period by law, or cannot meet because of an armed attack; the statute also describes removal when Congress directs it by concurrent resolution.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a narrow set of late-July 2026 escalatory, congressional, energy-market, Houthi, and ceasefire-related developments; it does not provide a complete account of the war’s origins, all military operations, humanitarian consequences, diplomacy, or legal disputes.

event_overview.title: About Papal Visits
event_overview.subject: Papal Visits
event_overview.summary: This event is part of Pope Leo XIV’s apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, a Vatican-organized pastoral visit running from November 6 to 17, 2026. The Argentina leg combines public liturgies and meetings with national authorities, church representatives, religious communities, workers, young people and social-service institutions, including a disability-care home in Claypole.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The apostolic journey is scheduled for November 6-17, 2026; the pope’s Argentina program runs from his arrival in Buenos Aires on November 8 until his departure for Lima on November 11.

facts.label: Organizer and format
facts.value: The Holy See’s Press Office published the official itinerary. It describes the trip as an apostolic journey of Pope Leo XIV to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, comprising pastoral, civic and interreligious engagements as well as Masses.

facts.label: Claypole visit
facts.value: On November 9, Leo visited the staff and residents of the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione de Claypole, a residential care center in Claypole, in Buenos Aires Province.

facts.label: Institution
facts.value: Don Orione Argentina describes the Claypole Cottolengo as its largest residential center in Argentina; it provides a home and care for people with disabilities and reports housing 415 residents.

facts.label: Stated pastoral purpose
facts.value: In his address to Argentine authorities, Leo said he came as successor of Saint Peter and as a pastor, to meet the church in Argentina and address the wider nation; at Claypole, he emphasized charity, welcome and the dignity of residents.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the Claypole welcome and the pope’s continuation of the Argentina portion of the trip, not the full Uruguay-Argentina-Peru itinerary or every event during the visit.
